Sales-Led Growth

When a product needs a human being to close the deal, and what that human being actually does.

On the second Tuesday of March 2025, Aditi Rao, VP of Product at the Bengaluru-based workforce-compliance software company Ekavira Systems, sat in a board meeting listening to a number she already knew by heart: eleven. That was the number of weeks a prospective customer, the Pune-and-Chennai auto-components manufacturer Elaan Manufacturing, had been sitting inside Ekavira's self-serve free trial without converting to a paid plan. Elaan's plant HR manager had signed up on a Thursday afternoon, explored the labour-law compliance dashboards for about forty minutes, invited the compliance head to look at it, and then the trial had gone quiet. Nobody had cancelled it. Nobody had bought it either.

Ekavira had built its reputation, and its first ₹38 crore of annual recurring revenue, on a product that sold itself: a factory HR manager could sign up with a work email, connect one plant's attendance data, and be running statutory compliance checks inside a day, no salesperson involved. That self-serve motion produced 78% of Ekavira's new logos. But it produced only 31% of new ARR, because the accounts that found the product this way were almost all single-plant operations paying an average of ₹1.8 lakh a year. Elaan ran fourteen plants. If Ekavira could sell Elaan the multi-plant edition of the product, the contract was worth an estimated ₹42 lakh a year — more than twenty times the self-serve average. But nobody at Elaan with the authority to sign a ₹42-lakh, multi-year commitment was ever going to do so by clicking "upgrade" inside a product trial. A compliance head, a plant CFO, a corporate legal counsel and a group CISO were all going to need to look at this decision before money moved, and none of them was going to find their way into a self-serve dashboard to do it. The board's growth target — ₹60 crore ARR by the end of FY27 — depended on Ekavira winning accounts that looked like Elaan. Aditi's problem was not a product problem. It was that Ekavira had never built the machine that sells to a buying committee, and she had to decide, in front of the board, whether it was time to build one.

The idea

The machine Aditi was missing has a name: sales-led growth, usually abbreviated SLG. Sales-led growth is a go-to-market motion in which a paid human being — a salesperson — is the mechanism that turns a prospect into a customer. The salesperson finds or is handed the prospect, qualifies whether the opportunity is real, runs a structured set of conversations to understand what the buyer needs and who else must agree, tailors a proposal and a demonstration to that buyer's specific situation, negotiates price and contract terms, and personally shepherds the deal through however many people at the buyer's organisation have to sign off before a purchase order exists. In exchange for the cost of employing that person, the seller gets something the product alone cannot supply: judgement about an ambiguous situation, customisation of the pitch to the buyer's specific fears, and a named human being who is accountable if the deal turns out to be wrong.

This is the oldest go-to-market motion in modern business software, not the newest. Its disciplines were formalised across the 1970s and 1980s inside companies like IBM, Xerox and later Oracle and Siebel Systems, and were written down as teachable method in books such as Miller Heiman's Strategic Selling (1985) and Neil Rackham's SPIN Selling (1988), both of which turned "selling" from an individual talent into a repeatable, coachable process with named stages. For decades this was simply called "selling" — there was no need for a qualifying adjective, because there was no other way to sell software of any consequence. The phrase "sales-led growth" only entered common use after 2016, when the venture investor Blake Bartlett at OpenView Partners popularised the term "product-led growth" to describe the self-serve motion that companies like Slack, Dropbox and Atlassian had used to grow without salespeople at all. Once the industry needed a name for the old model to contrast it with the new one, "sales-led growth" was the label that stuck. The one sentence Aditi could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: sales-led growth means a paid seller carries the buying decision through the account's committee and its approval chain, in exchange for the judgement and customisation the product cannot supply by itself.

How it actually works

The mechanics look deceptively like a funnel, but the useful way to see them is as a relay race with several implicit handoffs that most people never explain out loud. It begins with a target: either an inbound signal (someone at the account requested a demo, or, as with Elaan, started a trial that stalled) or an outbound target chosen because the account fits the ideal customer profile — in Elaan's case, a manufacturer with more than five plants and a known history of labour-inspection penalties. A sales development representative, or SDR, makes first contact and runs a short qualification conversation, usually structured around a checklist such as BANT (budget, authority, need, timeline) or the more rigorous MEDDIC (metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identify pain, champion). The SDR's entire job is to decide, cheaply, whether this is worth an account executive's much more expensive time — and to identify who inside the account actually has the pain, not just who answered the phone.

Figure 1. The visible funnel is the top row. The invisible layer that most training decks never draw is champion enablement — the account executive is rarely in the room when the compliance head argues the case to the CFO.

Once qualified, the deal moves to an account executive (AE), who runs discovery — a structured conversation, not a demo — to establish what specific problem the buyer needs solved, what it currently costs them not to solve it, and who besides the person in the room has to say yes. For Elaan, discovery surfaced that the real trigger was a ₹6 lakh labour-inspection penalty levied on one plant four months earlier, and that the actual economic buyer was not the HR manager who ran the trial but the group compliance head, who had never opened the product. This is the step most people skip past when they describe SLG casually: single-threading, where a seller only ever talks to one contact, is the single most common cause of stalled enterprise deals, because the one contact who likes the product frequently has no budget authority and no ability to move the deal through procurement alone. A competent AE "multi-threads" — builds relationships with the economic buyer, the technical evaluator and the legal or security reviewer independently, so the deal does not die if any one of them changes jobs or loses interest. After discovery comes a technical evaluation or proof-of-concept, often run jointly with a solutions engineer, followed by the stage that swallows the most calendar time and is discussed the least: procurement and legal review, where security questionnaires, data-processing agreements and payment terms get negotiated by people who have never seen the product demo and do not care to. Only after that does a contract get redlined, signed, and handed to customer success for onboarding — the point at which, notably, the sales-led motion ends and a different discipline, retention and expansion, begins.

A worked example

The tool sales teams actually use to reason about how fast this machine produces revenue is called sales velocity, and it is worth doing the arithmetic once by hand because the formula's four inputs are exactly the four levers a manager like Aditi has to pull. Sales velocity equals the number of open, qualified opportunities in the pipeline, multiplied by the win rate, multiplied by the average deal value, divided by the length of the average sales cycle. It answers a single, very practical question: at the current settings of these four dials, how much new revenue is this pipeline generating per month?

Suppose Ekavira stands up a two-person enterprise pod — one AE, one SDR — targeting accounts like Elaan. At any given time the pod is carrying 20 open, qualified opportunities. Historically, deals that reach the qualified stage close at a 25% rate. The average enterprise deal value, based on Elaan's profile, is ₹42 lakh. The average sales cycle, from qualification to signature, runs 4 months. The arithmetic: 20 opportunities × 0.25 win rate = 5 expected wins; 5 × ₹42,00,000 = ₹2,10,00,000 in expected value generated by that pipeline; divide by 4 months, and the pod is generating ₹52.5 lakh of new ARR per month.

Suppose the group CISO's security review and the corporate legal team's contract redlines — the procurement-and-legal stage almost nobody budgets calendar time for — stretch the average cycle from 4 months to 7. This is the arithmetic reason experienced sales leaders obsess over shortening the procurement and legal stage specifically, rather than trying to talk faster in the discovery call: a month saved late in the cycle is worth more than a month saved early, because it is a month saved on every deal moving through the pipeline at once, not just one.

Figure 2. A longer cycle can be offset only by a proportionate increase in qualified pipeline volume — here, 20 opportunities growing to 35 restores the original velocity despite the slower cycle.

There is a second pass worth running, because it shows the lever a manager actually has some control over. If Aditi cannot shorten the procurement stage — and legal and security review timelines are frequently outside a vendor's control — she can try to restore velocity by increasing the number of qualified opportunities the pod is carrying. Raising the pipeline from 20 to 35 opportunities, with the cycle still at 7 months, gives 35 × 0.25 = 8.75 expected wins, × ₹42,00,000 = ₹3,67,50,000, divided by 7 months, which comes back to ₹52.5 lakh per month — the original number, recovered entirely through pipeline volume rather than speed. The lesson embedded in the arithmetic is that a sales-led motion facing a structurally long cycle is not necessarily unhealthy; it simply has to run at higher pipeline volume to produce the same monthly revenue, which is exactly why enterprise sales organisations invest so heavily in outbound prospecting and account-based marketing to keep the top of that pipeline full.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Sales-led is not the same thing as "high-touch onboarding"

A product can have a white-glove, human-assisted onboarding experience — a customer success manager walking a new account through setup — without any of that being sales-led growth, because the purchase decision itself was still made through self-serve checkout. SLG specifically describes who closes the deal, not who helps after it closes. Ekavira's self-serve customers already got help from a support team during setup; what they never got was a human being negotiating the actual purchase.

It is a spectrum, not a switch

Few companies are purely product-led or purely sales-led. The realistic middle category, often called sales-assisted or hybrid, lets small accounts buy through self-serve checkout while an inside-sales rep proactively reaches out to accounts that show high product usage or hit a plan ceiling, offering to help rather than gatekeeping. Ekavira did not need to abandon its self-serve motion to serve Elaan; it needed to add a second motion on top of the first one, aimed only at the segment self-serve could not close.

The cost of sales has to be smaller than the value it unlocks

Sales-led growth is expensive per logo: a fully loaded AE, a share of an SDR's time, a solutions engineer's hours and the marketing spend that fed the pipeline all have to be paid before a contract is signed. That cost only makes sense against a deal large enough to amortise it. A rule of thumb used by many SaaS finance teams is that the fully loaded cost of acquiring a sales-led deal should be recoverable within twelve to eighteen months of that deal's gross margin; a ₹1.8 lakh self-serve account could never justify an AE's time, which is precisely why Elaan's ₹42 lakh potential, not Elaan's interest in the product, is what justified building the enterprise pod.

Sales-led growth can quietly rewrite the product roadmap

Once account executives are compensated on closing named accounts, the feature requests that reach product management stop being a representative sample of the customer base and start being whatever the three or four largest deals in the pipeline need to close this quarter. This is not a hypothetical risk; it is close to the default outcome unless product management deliberately tracks how often "must-have for this deal" requests actually recur across the wider customer base before committing engineering time to them.

It is routinely confused with account-based marketing

Account-based marketing, or ABM, is a demand-generation strategy that concentrates marketing spend on a short list of named target accounts rather than casting a wide net; sales-led growth is the selling motion that closes the deals ABM helps surface. The two are frequently bundled together in vendor pitches and conference talks, but a company can run ABM feeding a self-serve product, or run sales-led selling off inbound leads with no ABM at all — they are adjacent disciplines, not synonyms.

Nothing about closing the deal tells you whether the product is good

A skilled seller can close an account whose actual usage of the product turns out to be shallow, because the seller sold the vision, the roadmap promise, or the relationship rather than the delivered product. This is precisely why sales-led companies that ignore net revenue retention — how much of last year's sales-led revenue survives and grows this year, independent of new logos — can post an impressive quarter of bookings while quietly accumulating an unrenewable book of business. Sales-led growth measures how well you can persuade a committee to say yes; it says nothing on its own about whether that committee's users are still logging in eight months later.

Founder-led selling is not yet a motion

Many companies close their first ten or twenty enterprise-sized deals with the founder or a senior product leader doing the selling personally, relying on credibility and improvisation rather than a repeatable process. That is genuinely useful — it is how you learn what the qualification questions, the objections and the buying committee actually look like — but it is not sales-led growth until the process the founder improvised has been written down clearly enough that someone who is not the founder can run it and hit a comparable win rate. Aditi's board was, in effect, asking her whether Ekavira had that playbook yet, or only a handful of deals her own CEO had closed by force of personality.

The buying committee is not a single throat to choke

New sellers often treat the "champion" — the enthusiastic internal advocate, in Elaan's case the HR manager who ran the trial — as if persuading that one person is the whole job. In reality the champion's job is to persuade people the seller may never meet, in rooms the seller is never invited into. A seller's real work product is frequently a one-page internal document, a cost-justification email, or a slide the champion can forward, because the deal is often decided in a meeting where no one from the vendor is present at all.

In consumer products, sales-led growth is rare enough to be almost a contradiction in terms, because no individual consumer purchase is large enough to justify a human seller's time; where it does appear, it is usually a B2B2C arrangement — a wealth-management app that sells into employers as a workplace benefit, for instance, uses sales-led motion at the employer level even though the end user experience underneath is entirely self-serve. In B2B software, sales-led growth is the default for anything that requires integration with other systems, handles regulated data, or costs enough that a buyer needs internal sign-off simply to protect their own job if it fails — which describes Ekavira's compliance product exactly once it is being sold to a fourteen-plant manufacturer rather than a single HR manager. In marketplaces, the picture splits by side: the demand side (buyers) is very often self-serve, while the supply side — recruiting the sellers, restaurants, hospitals or lenders who populate the marketplace — is frequently sales-led, because a marketplace with no supply has nothing for a self-serve buyer to buy. The same product can therefore be product-led on one side of its own marketplace and sales-led on the other simultaneously.

Company stage changes the picture again. An early-stage company, before it has more than a handful of enterprise logos, typically cannot yet build a repeatable SLG motion at all, because a repeatable motion requires knowing which qualification questions predict a win, what objections recur, and what the buying committee typically looks like — none of which exists until enough deals have been run, however inefficiently, to notice the pattern. A large, mature company by contrast usually runs several motions side by side, segmented by account size, and treats moving an account from self-serve into the sales-led motion (or the reverse, when a large account wants to self-manage) as a deliberate operational decision with its own criteria, not an ad hoc judgement call by whichever employee happens to answer the account first.

Common mistakes

Hiring account executives before the playbook exists. The symptom is a new AE who closes almost nothing in their first two quarters despite being personally capable; the underlying error is asking someone to execute a repeatable process that has not yet been written down, forcing them to rediscover the ideal customer profile and the objection-handling script from scratch. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, before the first AE is hired, who inside the company has personally closed five comparable deals and can produce a written account of how — if the honest answer is nobody, the company is not ready to hire for the role, only to have someone senior run a few deals personally first.

Compensation plans that reward logos, not durable revenue. The symptom is bookings that look strong on a quarterly slide next to a renewal rate that quietly deteriorates a year later; the underlying error is paying commission entirely on new-logo signature with no clawback or renewal component, which rationally teaches sellers to close whatever will sign, whether or not it will renew. The cheapest diagnostic is to check whether the compensation plan pays out any differently for a customer who churns in month four versus one who is still active and expanding at month eighteen — if the answer is "no difference," the incentive is already misaligned.

Selling a roadmap that does not exist. The symptom is a customer success team inheriting an account whose contract explicitly or implicitly promised a feature that engineering never agreed to build; the underlying error is a seller under quota pressure treating "we could build that" as equivalent to "we will build that by the date I just told the customer." The cheapest diagnostic is a standing rule that any commitment to unreleased functionality requires a written sign-off from a product manager before it appears in a proposal or a verbal promise on a call.

Mistaking a rising average deal size for validated demand. The symptom is a sales leader proudly reporting that average contract value has doubled, when in fact the number of deals closed has fallen by the same proportion; the underlying error is treating ACV growth as an unambiguously good sign without checking whether it reflects genuinely larger accounts being won, or simply fewer, larger, harder-fought deals surviving a shrinking pipeline. The cheapest diagnostic is to look at total deal count and total pipeline volume alongside ACV every time the average is quoted, not the average in isolation.

What good looks like

Contrast Aditi's situation with Enakshi Health Systems, a Chennai-based hospital-billing software company that built its enterprise sales motion two years before it needed one at scale. Enakshi's first three enterprise deals were closed personally by its co-founder, who kept a private notebook of every qualification question that predicted a win and every objection that predicted a loss — not a formal document, just discipline about writing it down each time. By the fourth deal, that notebook had become a one-page qualification checklist; by the eighth, it was a documented discovery-call script and a list of the four roles that always turned out to matter at a hospital group (finance, IT security, the billing department, and, quietly, the doctor who chaired procurement). When Enakshi hired its first two account executives, it handed them that document on day one rather than asking them to reconstruct it from scratch, and both hit 80% of quota within two quarters — not because they were exceptional sellers, but because the company had already done the hard cognitive work of turning founder intuition into a teachable process before it hired anyone to execute it.

Closing

Aditi's recommendation to the board was not to abandon self-serve, and not to build a large enterprise sales team overnight. She proposed a single two-person pod — one AE, one SDR — targeting only accounts that looked like Elaan: five or more plants, a documented compliance-penalty history, and a self-serve trial that had stalled for more than four weeks, which her data showed was a reliable signal of a genuine multi-stakeholder deal rather than a curious individual. She asked for two quarters to write down, deal by deal, exactly what Enakshi had written down over two years, before deciding whether to hire a third seller. The board approved a pilot budget roughly equal to the fully loaded cost of the pod, sized against the arithmetic in Table 1: even at the stretched 7-month cycle, one pod's velocity of ₹30 lakh a month, sustained for two quarters, would clear the pilot's cost several times over if even a handful of accounts the size of Elaan actually closed.

What Aditi still needed to learn next, and told the board so directly, was how to tell in advance which accounts belonged in the sales-led motion and which belonged in self-serve — the topic of choosing a go-to-market motion — and how to design the trigger that would move a self-serve account, mid-life, into a sales conversation once its usage crossed a threshold, which is the logic behind product-qualified leads and product-led sales. Both extend directly from the distinction this topic exists to draw: not every product needs salespeople, but every product that asks a committee, not an individual, to say yes, eventually does.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. If your product's largest and smallest customers pay wildly different amounts for what is functionally the same software, at what price point does a human seller's time stop being a rounding error and start being the deciding factor in whether the deal closes at all?

2. When a founder closes the first ten enterprise deals personally, what exactly has to be written down — and by whom — before that founder's judgement can be called a repeatable sales motion rather than a personality?

Prakhar Latex Networks: Does the Product Need Salespeople?

A teaching case on sales-led growth

1. Opening

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Cherian Kuruvilla sat in the second-floor conference room of Prakhar Latex Networks, above a rubber-dealers' street in Kottayam, with a printed spreadsheet and a decision due in three days. The board would meet on Friday, 9 October, at the start of the post-monsoon tapping season, and Kuruvilla, the company's chief executive and co-founder, had promised it a single recommendation: should Prakhar hire a field sales team to sell its software to India's large rubber processors, or keep growing the way it always had, with a product that dealers sign up for by themselves?

It was urgent because a Dubai trading house, one of the largest buyers of processed rubber that Prakhar's customers supplied, had asked for a written traceability plan by the end of the month, and that plan could not be delivered by a website.

2. Company background

Prakhar was founded in 2019 by Kuruvilla, a former procurement manager at a Kottayam latex concentrate factory, and two engineers. Its product, Nabh Kanta Cloud, digitises the moment when a processor buys raw material from a smallholder or a dealer. A weighbridge reading and a dry rubber content test are captured on a phone, the payable amount is computed, and the money is sent by UPI, then reconciled and posted to Tally or Zoho Books with the GST paperwork attached.

Kerala grows most of India's natural rubber, and the Rubber Board, headquartered in Kottayam, supports the industry. Demand comes from tyre makers such as MRF, Apollo Tyres, CEAT and JK Tyre. Prakhar's competitors were mostly spreadsheets and ledgers, and consultants who built one-off workflows on Zoho Creator. Payments ran on NPCI's UPI rails, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, meant grower records needed consent handling.

By September 2026 Prakhar had 1,935 paying accounts and annual recurring revenue of ₹16.08 crore, spread across three very different kinds of customer, summarised in Exhibit 1. Growth had come from dealer word of mouth, a self-serve sign-up flow, and Kuruvilla himself, who had sold all fifteen large accounts over dinners in Changanassery and Kanjirappally.

3. The situation

The 1,800 small dealers were 93.0 per cent of the accounts but only 40.3 per cent of the revenue, and they left at a rate of 25 per cent a year, which cost ₹1.62 crore of ARR annually. The fifteen large processors were less than one per cent of the accounts, yet brought in 26.1 per cent of the revenue and left at 4 per cent. Every large account paid ₹28 lakh a year, seventy-eight times what a dealer paid.

The trouble was that large processors did not sign up on a website. Prakhar estimated that India had 75 processors above 500 tonnes a month, so 60 remained unsold. Each had a purchasing committee, a finance head wanting the Tally integration proved on live data, a compliance officer asking about DPDP consent, and a tyre-maker customer demanding plot-level traceability. Dinners had worked at fifteen accounts; they would not work at sixty.

Three of the company's people saw the problem from different time zones. In Singapore, the customer-success lead reported that dealer churn peaked after the monsoon, when small buyers reverted to paper. In Toronto, the data scientist had analysed usage and found that self-serve dealers who never used the UPI payout feature within thirty days accounted for most of the churn. In New Jersey, the head of enterprise sales had been running a pilot with one large Changanassery processor for three months, and believed six wins in a year were realistic.

4. The people

Cherian Kuruvilla (chief executive, Kottayam) wanted growth that did not endanger the company's cash. He distrusted a payroll built on one pilot.

Varun Kaimal (head of enterprise sales, New Jersey) had sold commodity software to multinationals before joining four months earlier. He argued that a ₹28 lakh product needs a person beside the buyer, and that waiting would let a competitor claim the processors.

Jossy Panicker (head of product, Bengaluru) feared that salespeople would promise custom features to close deals and turn a clean product into a services business. She preferred to improve onboarding and keep dealers self-serve.

Padmini Nambiar (customer-success lead, Singapore) spoke for the dealers. She doubted one support model could serve both a ₹36,000 dealer and a ₹28 lakh processor. In Toronto, the data scientist Preethi Nair supplied the churn analysis but took no side.

5. The options

Option A: build the sales team. Hire the five people in Exhibit 2 and target the sixty unsold large processors. The upside is 24 pilots and six contracts, in the highest-retention segment. The cost is ₹1.18 crore, nine months before any contract, and a risk that the team sells promises engineering cannot keep.

Option B: stay self-serve. Spend ₹40 lakh on onboarding, in-app UPI payout prompts and dealer marketing. The Kerala dealer pool is nearly tapped, so Prakhar expected 250 new dealers, worth ₹90 lakh of new ARR. It is cheap, but it feeds the segment that churns at 25 per cent and cannot reach a purchasing committee.

Option C: partner through tyre makers. Spend ₹18 lakh on a partnerships manager and integrations, and ask tyre makers to encourage their approved processors to adopt Nabh Kanta Cloud for traceability. If ten mid processors came this way, the new ARR would be ₹45 lakh. It is inexpensive, but the volume depends on companies Prakhar does not control, and no tyre maker has yet agreed to anything.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 say about which customers deserve a salesperson, and which do not?
  2. Why did founder-led selling work for fifteen accounts and why will it not scale to sixty?
  3. Exhibit 4 ranks the options differently by efficiency and by total retained ARR. Which measure should the board use, and why?
  4. If you chose to hire, what would you fund now, what would you hold back, and what evidence would release the remainder?

7. A note for the learner

Sales-led growth is the go-to-market motion in which people, not the product alone, move a buyer from interest to contract. It fits when the price is high, the buyer is a committee, the value depends on the buyer's own numbers, and the product must be fitted into their systems. Each holds for Prakhar's large processors and fails for its small dealers. The lens is therefore not "sales or no sales" but "which customers, and what must change in the company when a salesperson arrives."

One defensible path is a staged version of Option A, kept alongside the existing self-serve flow for dealers. The arithmetic supports it in a way the first-year ratio hides. A large account's ₹28 lakh, churning at 4 per cent, is still worth ₹22.83 lakh a year after five years, while a dealer's ₹0.36 lakh, churning at 25 per cent, has shrunk to about ₹8,543. The first-year ratio penalises Option A for a cost that is mostly fixed and front-loaded, and Options B and C cannot reach the sixty accounts at all.

A teaching case on sales-led growth. Nagpur, November 2026.

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Gauri Wankhede was still in the Sankalan Flock Systems office on Central Bazar Road in Nagpur, windows open to the cold. The board met at ten the next morning, and had asked her for one thing: whether to build a field sales organisation, and if so, how large.

Two documents lay on the table. The first was a plan from Falguni Deshmukh, the head of enterprise sales, hired in June and working out of New Jersey: eight people, ₹244 lakh in the first year, aimed at integrators Sankalan had never reached by any other means. The second was a note from Madhura Gawande, the head of product in Bengaluru, which did not argue against salespeople. It argued that the company did not yet know what its own numbers meant, and that a sales team would freeze that ignorance into a payroll.

Wankhede's difficulty was that both documents were built from the same nine contracts, and she had begun to suspect those nine were not a sample of a market but a sample of her father's address book.

2. How the company came to be shaped this way

Sankalan was founded by Wankhede, then a production planner at a Vidarbha feed mill, and Milind Bhoyar, an engineer from a Pune plant-floor software firm. Their product, Sankalan Shed, began as a tablet application for a broiler shed: daily mortality, feed issued, weight samples, medication events, and a running feed conversion ratio against a standard curve. A module added in 2021 reconciled the flock record against the feed mill's despatch ledger, so a contract farmer's settlement could be computed, paid over UPI, and posted to Tally or Zoho Books with the GST invoice attached.

By 2026 Sankalan had 2,835 paying accounts and annual recurring revenue of ₹2,198.40 lakh, just under ₹22 crore, as Exhibit 1 shows. The independent farmers signed up on the website, paid through Razorpay, and never spoke to anyone. The nine integrators had each been sold in person, over months, by Wankhede.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in March 2023. Rachit Agro Proteins of Wardha, the first integrator, was then the only reason payroll was met, and its general manager, Ganesh Dhande, would sign only on terms his legal department drafted. Schedule C gave Rachit an eighteen-month exclusivity window on any feature built at its request, and a most-favoured-customer clause resetting Rachit's price downward if Sankalan ever charged a comparable integrator less. Wankhede needed the signature and agreed. Neither clause seemed expensive with one integrator. Both are now the arithmetic of the sales plan.

3. The industry

Indian broiler production is organised around integrators. A company such as Venky's, Suguna Foods, Godrej Agrovet or the IB Group owns the hatchery and the feed mill, places day-old chicks with contract farmers, supplies feed on its own account, and buys the grown bird back at a contracted rate per kilogram. The farmer supplies the shed and the labour; the integrator carries the price risk on maize and soymeal, which moved violently through 2025 and 2026, and on bird price.

Three forces had lately made flock data worth money. Quick-commerce and meat-delivery buyers — Licious, Swiggy Instamart, Zepto — wanted batch-level traceability on chilled chicken. FSSAI had tightened expectations on antibiotic residue records. And European buying groups sourcing through APEDA channels wanted welfare and medication audit trails no paper register could produce. Marijke van der Velde, a Rotterdam auditor for one such group, had told Dhande in September that a second audit failure would end Rachit's European line.

Against that, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 had made contract-farmer records a consent question every compliance officer now raised. Sankalan's competition was not other software but Excel, a consultant's Zoho Creator app, and the integrator's own IT department, which in three of the nine accounts had proposed building the thing in-house.

Through 2024 and 2025 the belief inside the company was simple and attractive. Independent farmers churned; integrators did not. Not one had ever cancelled. Sales-Led Growth at Depth

What the motion costs, where its arithmetic breaks, and the disagreements nobody has settled.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 14 August 2025, in a converted textile shed off the Mumbai–Pune expressway that Laghima Robotics uses as its integration floor, Rohan Mahajan watched a six-axis palletising cell put its four-thousandth carton onto a pallet without a fault and felt no relief at all. Mahajan is Laghima's Chief Product Officer. The cell on the floor was not the problem. The problem was the spreadsheet his CFO had sent him the previous evening, which showed that Laghima's field sales organisation — six account executives, two solutions engineers, one sales-development representative and a newly hired VP of Sales — had consumed ₹14.9 crore in the eighteen months since the board approved the enterprise build-out, and had closed ₹18.3 crore of bookings against a plan of ₹42 crore.

Laghima sells a warehouse robotics system: a fleet of autonomous mobile robots, a floor-side controller, and a software layer that plans routes, reconciles inventory and exposes an API to whatever warehouse management system the customer already runs. A typical deal is ₹98 lakh of hardware, installed, plus ₹22 lakh a year of recurring software and support. The buying committee at a customer like Lakshan Alloys, the Raipur steel processor Laghima had been working for seven months, runs to eleven named people: the plant head who wants it, the operations director who owns the P&L, the corporate engineering group that must certify it, the IT security team that must let it onto the network, a finance controller who must find capex in a year when capex is being cut, a safety officer, two union representatives who must be consulted before any change to the shop floor's work allocation, the group CIO, a procurement manager, and — a detail that had cost Laghima four weeks — the insurer's risk surveyor, whose sign-off the plant needed before its liability cover would extend to an unmanned vehicle operating near human pickers.

Mahajan's board wanted a recommendation in three weeks: double down on field sales, or cut it back and sell through system integrators. The VP of Sales had a confident answer, which was that the team was under-ramped and under-supported and that the plan should be re-based, not abandoned. Mahajan did not think she was lying. He also did not think she was right, and he could not yet articulate why.

Bengaluru, 2 September 2025.

Nineteen days later and 840 kilometres south, Meera Sundaram, co-founder and head of product at Lipika Intelligence, was reading a different spreadsheet with the opposite problem. Lipika sells an AI-native contract intelligence product: it ingests a lender's loan agreements, sanction letters and security documents, extracts obligations and covenants, and flags divergences from the approved template. It is priced by consumption — a rate per thousand pages processed, on an annual committed minimum. Lipika's eleven enterprise customers had signed contracts worth ₹4.2 crore of annual committed value. At month six, actual consumption across those eleven accounts was running at an annualised ₹1.85 crore, or 44% of what had been contracted.

Lipika's sales team had done exactly what it was paid to do. Commission was 9% of contracted annual value, so the team had earned ₹37.8 lakh on the ₹4.2 crore booked. Against realised revenue, the same rate would have earned ₹16.7 lakh. Lipika had, in effect, paid ₹21.1 lakh — eleven percent of every rupee it actually collected — for revenue that had not happened. Sundaram's CRO, Anand Kulkarni, argued that consumption always lags in year one and that the committed minimums would be billed anyway at true-up. Lipika's largest customer, the Mumbai non-banking financial company Lopamudra Finserv, had already asked, informally, whether the minimum could be renegotiated downward at renewal rather than paid on paper for pages it had not processed.

Both companies had done what the standard advice says to do. Both had built the motion, hired the people, written the playbook. Neither was in obvious trouble and both were losing money in ways their dashboards did not show. What follows is an attempt to say precisely why — and what an expert sees in these two situations that a competent practitioner does not.

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

Sales-led growth is a go-to-market motion in which a compensated human being is the mechanism by which a prospective buyer becomes a customer. That definition is settled and uninteresting. What is not settled is why that human being is necessary, and the five serious answers to that question produce five different companies.

The first answer is informational: the buyer cannot evaluate the product without help, because the product's value depends on facts about the buyer's own environment that the buyer has not assembled. The second is political: the buyer can evaluate the product perfectly well but cannot get the organisation to act, and the seller's real product is internal persuasion carried out by proxy. The third is actuarial: a large purchase is a career risk for whoever signs it, and a named vendor representative is a form of insurance — someone to call, someone to blame, someone whose own reputation is on the line. The fourth is economic: the seller exists because the deal is large enough to amortise a seller's cost, and for no other reason. The fifth is historical: the seller exists because the category has always been sold that way and the buyer's procurement process assumes a vendor representative will be present.

These are not alternative framings of one idea. They give different answers to operational questions. If the reason is informational, the correct investment is in solutions engineering and in product telemetry that lets a buyer evaluate themselves — and the seller's headcount should fall as the product improves. If the reason is political, the correct investment is in the artefacts a champion carries into rooms the seller never enters, and headcount should fall only if the buyer's org chart flattens, which it will not. If the reason is actuarial, the correct investment is in references, indemnities and the vendor's own balance sheet, and the seller is nearly irreplaceable. If the reason is purely economic, the seller is a line item to be optimised away at the first opportunity. If the reason is historical, the seller is a tax on the category that the first competitor with a credible alternative will collect instead.

The intellectual history maps onto these answers. The process school — Miller Heiman's Strategic Selling (1985), the MEDDIC family of qualification frameworks developed at PTC in the 1990s, and more recently Jacco van der Kooij's revenue-architecture work — treats selling as a manufacturing process in which variance is the enemy. It would sign the proposition that a documented stage model with hard exit criteria raises win rate independent of individual rep talent. It would not sign the proposition that method can substitute for product-market fit; its own practitioners are the first to say that a rigorous process applied to a product nobody needs simply produces rigorous losses faster.

The insight school — the Corporate Executive Board's study of several thousand sellers, published by Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson as The Challenger Sale in 2011 — holds that the highest performers teach the buyer something about the buyer's own business, tailor that teaching to the individual stakeholder, and take control of the commercial conversation, and that the "relationship builder" profile is the worst-performing of the five they identified. It would sign the proposition that commercial teaching creates preference before an RFP exists, and that a deal shaped at specification-writing time is largely decided. It would not sign the proposition that being liked wins deals.

The economics school — Mark Leslie and Charles Holloway's "The Sales Learning Curve" (Harvard Business Review, 2006), Peter Thiel's insistence in Zero to One that distribution is a product decision, and the unit-economics literature that grew up around SaaS boards after 2010 — treats the whole question as capital allocation. It would sign the proposition that the only defensible reason to hire the nth seller is that the nth seller's post-ramp contribution exceeds their fully loaded cost. It would not sign the proposition that a better methodology can rescue unit economics that do not work; it would say the methodology is a rounding error against the gross margin and the deal size.

The buyer-sovereignty school — the product-led growth literature that OpenView's Blake Bartlett named in 2016, reinforced by Gartner's buyer-side surveys showing that a substantial share of B2B buyers say they would prefer to complete a purchase with no vendor representative involved at all — holds that the seller is friction the buyer tolerates rather than value the buyer wants. It would sign the proposition that any step a buyer can complete unaided should be removed from the seller's job. It would not sign the proposition that a committee will approve a multi-crore, multi-year commitment with no human counterparty; its strongest advocates concede that the signature itself is the last thing to be automated, and some concede it never will be.

The trust school is the oldest and, in India, the most commercially consequential, because the distributor and channel traditions that shaped Indian industrial selling were built on multi-decade personal relationships rather than on quarterly territory assignments. It holds that in long-cycle, high-consequence purchases the seller is underwriting the buyer's personal risk, and that the asset being accumulated is trust, which does not transfer when a rep resigns. It would sign the proposition that named-account continuity beats territory optimisation. It would not sign the proposition that CRM hygiene is ever the binding constraint on a sales organisation's performance.

The camps are not describing different industries. They are describing the same deal and disagreeing about what the money is buying. An expert can tell you, for a specific deal, which of the five explanations is operative — and will notice when the answer changes mid-cycle.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic underneath the funnel

The stage model — qualification, discovery, evaluation, procurement, close — is familiar. What separates practitioners is the quantitative treatment of three things the stage model does not contain: the structure of committee assent, the capacity a sales organisation actually has as opposed to the capacity its headcount implies, and the margin consequences of the discretion sellers are given.

3.1 Committee assent is multiplicative, and that changes what to buy

Treat each required approver at an account as an independent gate with probability p of assent. The probability of the deal clearing all n gates is pn. This is a crude model and its independence assumption is wrong in an interesting way, but the crude version already produces a result most sellers get backwards.

Figure 1. Joint assent under the independence assumption. At p = 0.85, a five-approver committee clears at 44% and a three-approver committee at 61%. The curves matter less than their shape: the penalty for each additional approver is proportional, so it compounds, while the benefit of making each approver marginally happier is linear in the exponent.

Take Laghima's deal at Lakshan Alloys. Suppose Mahajan's team could make every one of the eleven named stakeholders 85% likely to assent — an unrealistically good state of affairs. The joint probability would be 0.8511, or 17%. Reduce the required approvers to five and the same enthusiasm yields 44%. Now consider the two levers as investments. Removing one approver from a committee of five multiplies the joint probability by 1/p, a 17.6% relative gain at p = 0.85. To achieve the same gain by raising enthusiasm, every one of the five approvers must move from 0.85 to 0.885 — three and a half percentage points each, simultaneously, on people the seller may never meet.

That is the counter-intuitive result: reducing the approval surface is usually cheaper than raising enthusiasm, and almost no sales methodology is organised around it. Reducing the approval surface is mostly a product and commercial-terms activity, not a selling activity. Laghima's insurance-surveyor gate existed because the robots operated in mixed human-robot zones; a software-configurable exclusion zone, shipped in the product, would have removed a gate entirely rather than trying to charm it. A data-residency commitment written into the standard contract removes the group CISO from the critical path at a dozen accounts at once. A pre-signed master services agreement with a common redline bank removes legal from the critical path everywhere. Each of those is a one-time engineering or legal investment that lowers n permanently across the whole pipeline, and each competes for budget with hiring another seller, which raises pipeline volume but does nothing to n.

The independence assumption is where the model is wrong, and the way it is wrong is the champion. In practice, approvals are correlated: a respected internal advocate raises several gates together, and a single influential sceptic lowers several together. In the limiting case of perfect correlation, the joint probability is simply p, regardless of n — which is exactly what a seller experiences when a powerful champion carries the whole committee, and exactly what makes single-threaded deals feel deceptively easy right up to the moment the champion changes jobs. The correct mental model is therefore not "multiply the gates" but "estimate how much of the committee is correlated through one person, and treat that correlation as the largest single risk in the deal." An expert asks, of any deal with an enthusiastic champion: if this person left tomorrow, how many of these eleven approvals survive?

The single most important line in Table 1 is the attainment row, and it is the one most boards never interrogate. Quota attainment across a sales organisation is not normally distributed. It is right-skewed, with a long upper tail: a small number of sellers close two or three times quota, usually because they inherited a large installed base or caught a single transformational deal, and they drag the arithmetic mean far above the median. Laghima's VP of Sales quoted 78% because that was the mean of the benchmark data she had. Planning a new team off mean attainment over-forecasts by the entire skew of the distribution — in Laghima's case, roughly ₹8.6 crore before the ramp and attrition adjustments are even applied.

Compound that with ramp. A field seller in a nine-month cycle contributes nothing in their first two quarters not because they are lazy but because the deals they start in month one close in month ten. A capacity plan that hires four sellers in-year and credits them with full-year quota is not optimistic; it is arithmetically impossible, because it assumes a cycle length of zero. Laghima's plan implicitly assumed that. The gap between ₹42.1 crore and ₹19.9 crore is not a performance failure. It is a modelling failure, and the actual result of ₹18.3 crore sits within 8% of the honest model — which is to say the sales team performed roughly as expected and was told it had failed by 57%.

This has a second-order consequence that is more damaging than the miss itself. When a team is told it has failed by a margin it never had the capacity to cover, the rational response is to pull deals forward by discounting, to sandbag the following quarter's forecast so that the next miss is smaller, and for the best sellers — who can read a distribution — to leave. Attrition rises, which further reduces effective capacity, which produces a larger miss. Laghima was two quarters into that loop when Mahajan got the spreadsheet.

3.3 Discount authority is a margin-structure decision, not a sales-policy decision

The third piece of arithmetic concerns the discretion a company gives sellers. Almost every sales organisation has a discount approval matrix: a rep may go to 15% unaided, a director to 25%, the CRO to 40%. These thresholds are almost always set by copying another company, and they are almost always wrong, because the margin consequence of a given discount depends entirely on the cost structure underneath the list price.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

The decision to run a sales-led motion can be reduced to four claims, each of which can be checked against data rather than asserted. Applied to the two protagonists, they produce different verdicts.

Claim one: the annual contract value clears the fully loaded cost of sale by a multiple large enough to survive the win rate. The relevant number is not the cost of a closed deal but the cost of a pursued deal divided by the win rate. Laghima's pod cost per pursuit was approximately ₹7.8 lakh; at a 32% win rate, the cost of sale per closed deal was ₹24.4 lakh plus ₹7 lakh of allocated marketing, against a first-year contract of ₹1.2 crore. The claim holds, comfortably. Lipika's cost of sale per closed deal was ₹9.1 lakh against a contracted ₹38 lakh — but against realised first-year revenue of ₹16.7 lakh, the cost of sale was 54% of revenue. The claim holds on contracted value and fails on realised value, and which of those two numbers is the real one is the argument Sundaram and Kulkarni were having.

Figure 2. Each motion's cost of sale falls as a share of contract value, but only crosses into viability at a specific contract size. Where the dashed 25% ceiling is crossed — ₹72,000 for self-serve, ₹10.4 lakh for inside sales, ₹1.04 crore for a field motion — is the threshold at which that motion begins to make sense. Laghima at ₹1.2 crore sits just past the field threshold. Lipika at ₹38 lakh contracted sits well short of it, and would be viable only as an inside-sales motion.

Claim two: the purchase requires assent from more than one person with independent authority to stop it. This is the political test, and it is the one that most reliably predicts whether a self-serve motion will stall. Laghima passes overwhelmingly: eleven gates, of which at least four — security, safety, the insurer, the union consultation — can veto unilaterally. Lipika passes too, but less severely: four gates at Lopamudra Finserv, of which the Reserve Bank of India's outsourcing and IT-governance expectations make the chief risk officer's review non-negotiable. This is why Lipika could not simply become self-serve even though its deal sizes suggested inside sales; a regulated lender cannot onboard a vendor that processes loan documents without a documented third-party risk assessment, whatever the price.

Claim three: the buyer cannot establish value without help that the product cannot supply. Laghima passes: no warehouse manager can predict throughput gain without a site survey of aisle widths, rack heights, floor flatness and pick-path density. Lipika fails, and this is the crux of its problem. A lender can upload a hundred agreements and see for itself, in an afternoon, what the extraction accuracy is. Lipika's product could demonstrate its own value better than any account executive could describe it, which means Lipika's sellers were being paid to do something the product already did, and the resulting deals were sold on projected volumes rather than demonstrated ones — which is precisely why consumption came in at 44%.

Claim four: the motion is repeatable, meaning someone other than the founder has closed comparable deals using written criteria. Neither company clearly passes. Laghima's two tenured sellers had both been hired from robotics competitors and were closing on personal relationships built over a decade; nothing they knew had been written down, and the four new hires were reconstructing it from scratch. Lipika's playbook existed but described the wrong motion.

There is a fifth situation worth naming, in which the idea of sales-led growth is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading: when a company's revenue concentration means that what looks like a motion is actually a handful of relationships. A company with ₹30 crore of revenue from nine accounts does not have a sales-led growth motion; it has nine accounts. Every metric computed on that base — win rate, cycle time, attainment — has a sample size too small to be a signal, and building a capacity plan on those numbers, as Laghima did, produces the confident nonsense in the left-hand column of Table 1.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Hardware plus software. Laghima's category breaks two conventions at once. First, the capex/opex split means the buyer's approval path forks: the hardware goes through a capital appropriation process with its own committee and its own annual budget window, while the software subscription goes through an operating budget that can be approved by someone two levels lower. Sophisticated sellers in this category deliberately restructure the commercial terms — robots-as-a-service, with the hardware capitalised on the vendor's balance sheet — not because the customer prefers it but because it collapses two approval paths into one. That restructuring transfers working-capital risk onto the vendor, which is why it is a CFO decision dressed as a pricing decision. Second, the CAC-payback convention that SaaS boards use assumes all gross profit is recurring. Laghima's first-year gross profit per deal is ₹26.5 lakh of one-time hardware margin plus ₹18.5 lakh of recurring software margin. Counting both, CAC of ₹31 lakh pays back in about eight months and the motion looks excellent. Counting only recurring margin, payback is twenty months and the motion looks marginal. Both calculations are defensible; the board and the CPO were using different ones without either noticing.

AI-native products. Lipika's category breaks the relationship between a signature and revenue. In a seat-based subscription, a signed contract is very nearly revenue: the customer has committed to a number that does not depend on their behaviour. In a consumption model, the contract is an option the customer may decline to exercise, and the quota system — built for the seat world — pays out as though the option were certain. The second-order effect is worse than the commission leakage: a seller compensated on contracted value has a rational interest in selling the largest commitment the buyer will sign, which maximises the probability of a painful true-up conversation at renewal, which is the single most reliable destroyer of a renewal. Third, gross margin in an AI-native product is a function of how the customer uses it, not of what they paid, so the standard discount matrix (Table 2) is dangerous, and the rational policy floor is a margin floor expressed in cost-per-unit terms. Fourth, the proof-of-concept becomes a cost centre: a pilot that processes 40,000 pages costs real inference money, and a company running twelve simultaneous pilots to fill a pipeline is paying cost of goods sold to generate leads.

Two-sided marketplaces. Here the motion splits by side, and the seam between the two sides is where value is destroyed quietly. Lohagara Metals Exchange, a Kolkata B2B platform for secondary steel, runs a self-serve demand side of some 3,100 registered buyers and a field-sold supply side of 140 mills and stockists. Each onboarded supplier contributes, on average, ₹2.6 crore of annual gross merchandise value at a 1.1% take rate: ₹2.86 lakh of net revenue a year, against a supplier acquisition cost of ₹1.9 lakh. Payback of eight months; the board approved twelve more field reps. What the average concealed is that the top twelve suppliers produce 61% of GMV, and the bottom quartile of sales-acquired suppliers never crosses ₹40 lakh of annual GMV — ₹44,000 of net revenue — against the same ₹1.9 lakh acquisition cost. With supply-side churn at 31%, the expected lifetime value of a bottom-quartile supplier is roughly ₹1.4 lakh, well below what it cost to sign them. Lohagara was destroying value on perhaps 40% of its sales-led acquisitions while the blended payback number looked exemplary. The tell in a marketplace is always the same: any unit economic computed on the mean of a power-law distribution is meaningless, and marketplace supply is always a power law.

Regulated and public-sector selling. In India this deserves separate treatment because the mechanism is different rather than merely slower. When the buyer is a public sector undertaking or a government department procuring through the Government e-Marketplace, the commercial contest is frequently decided at the moment the technical specification is written, months before any tender is published; once published, award typically follows the lowest technically-qualified bid. Value-based selling — the entire apparatus of quantifying benefit and defending price — has no surface to act on at the bidding stage, because price is the only variable left. The consequence is that the field motion for this segment is not a selling motion at all but a specification-influence and empanelment motion, staffed by different people with different skills and measured on a different metric: not win rate, but the share of published tenders whose specifications the company can already meet at list price. Adjacent to this, the requirement that buyers settle micro and small enterprise invoices within statutory timelines has changed the cash dynamics for small vendors selling into large Indian corporates, and a vendor whose payment terms are now structurally faster has a real, if unglamorous, commercial advantage it should be pricing into the deal rather than conceding for free.

Figure 3. The four seams. Each is a handoff between functions with different metrics, and value leaks at each one because no single person's compensation spans the boundary. Mature companies do not eliminate the seams; they instrument them, which means putting a number on each gap and reviewing it monthly with both owners in the room.

What mature companies actually do at these seams, as opposed to what they say, is worth stating plainly. They say they have "alignment between sales and product." What they actually have, in the good cases, is a written promise ledger — a record of every commitment to unreleased functionality made in any proposal, with a named product manager's sign-off and a date — and a quarterly reconciliation of that ledger against what shipped. In the bad cases, and these are the majority, the ledger exists only in the memory of the customer success manager who inherits the account and discovers the promise when the customer invokes it.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The mean of a skewed distribution is a lie, and attainment is always skewed. The tell-tale sign is a sales leader quoting a single average attainment figure with no distribution behind it. The obvious reading — that a team at 78% of quota is 78% healthy — is wrong because that figure is typically produced by two sellers at 190% and six at 45%. The expert asks for the median and the interquartile range before accepting any capacity plan, and knows that the marginal hire lands near the median by construction.

Pipeline coverage must be stage-weighted and cohort-dated. The tell-tale sign is a confident "we are at 3.4x coverage" with no breakdown. The obvious reading is that 3.4 times the target sitting in pipeline is comfortable at a 30% win rate. It is wrong when most of that coverage was created in the last thirty days and sits in the first stage, because early-stage pipeline in a nine-month cycle cannot close in the quarter it is being counted against. The expert weights each stage by its historical conversion and by whether it can physically close inside the window, and usually finds that a 3.4x number is a 1.1x number.

Cycle time is a property of the buyer's calendar, not of the seller's energy. The tell-tale sign is deals slipping by exactly one quarter, repeatedly, across different sellers and different accounts. The obvious reading is poor closing discipline. The real cause is usually that the buyer's capital appropriation committee meets quarterly, or that the Indian fiscal year ending 31 March creates a March scramble and an April vacuum, and no amount of urgency manufactured by a seller moves a committee's meeting date. The expert maps the buyer's governance calendar during discovery and plans the close around it rather than against it.

The champion's binding constraint is career risk, not budget. The tell-tale sign is a champion who has been enthusiastic for months and goes quiet within days of an internal reorganisation announcement, a new boss, or a bad quarter at their own company. The obvious reading is that they lost interest or that a competitor got to them. The real reason is that the personal cost of sponsoring an unproven vendor rose, and it rose for reasons the seller has no visibility into. The expert's response is not to push harder but to lower the champion's personal exposure — a smaller first phase, a reference call with a peer in an identical role, a written success criterion the champion can point to if challenged.

Approvals are correlated, and the champion is the correlating device. The tell-tale sign is a deal that has been forecast at 80% for three consecutive months on the strength of one relationship. The obvious reading is that a strong champion de-risks a deal. It does the opposite to the variance: it converts eleven partially independent risks into one large one. The expert tests correlation directly by asking the champion to arrange a meeting with a stakeholder who is known to be sceptical, and reads the champion's willingness to do so as the real forecast signal.

Discount authority belongs to the margin structure, not to the org chart. The tell-tale sign is a single company-wide discount matrix applied across product lines with materially different cost of goods. The obvious reading is that consistency is fair and administratively simple. It is wrong because, as Table 2 shows, the same 35% costs six margin points on pure software and twenty-five on a hardware bundle. The expert sets authority in margin points and makes the deal desk surface the rupee gross-profit consequence at the moment of approval.

Roadmap capture is measurable, and "customer-driven" is not a defence when n equals one. The tell-tale sign is a product organisation that cannot answer the question "what share of this quarter's committed engineering capacity is traceable to a single named account?" The obvious reading is that building what customers ask for is virtuous. It is wrong when the request has been made by exactly one customer, has no recurrence data behind it, and arrived attached to a quarter-end deal. The expert tracks this ratio explicitly — most healthy enterprise software companies sit between 10% and 25% — and treats anything above a third as a signal that sales is setting strategy.

Won-deal reviews teach more than lost-deal reviews. The tell-tale sign is a company with a formal loss-review process and no equivalent for wins. The obvious reading is that you learn from failure. It is incomplete because losses are usually over-attributed to price, which is the easiest thing for a losing buyer to say and the hardest to verify, whereas wins frequently turn out to have been caused by something entirely outside the playbook — a regulatory deadline, an incumbent's outage, a personal connection — and knowing which of those it was determines whether the win is repeatable. The expert runs both, and treats an unexplained win as an unresolved risk.

Motion is a property of a segment and a moment, not of a company. The tell-tale sign is a strategy document that says "we are moving from product-led to sales-led." The obvious reading is that a company graduates from one motion to another. It is wrong because the same account frequently travels in both directions: a self-serve team expands into a committee purchase and moves into a sales-led motion, then, three years later, standardises and asks to self-manage its own renewals and seat administration, moving back. The expert designs the triggers for movement in both directions and treats them as operational rules rather than judgement calls.

A signed contract is neither revenue nor cash. The tell-tale sign is a bookings number celebrated in a board deck with no adjacent figure for consumption, collection or days sales outstanding. The obvious reading is that the contract is the achievement. It is wrong in a consumption model, where the contract is an option the customer may not exercise, and it is wrong in the Indian mid-market generally, where ninety-day and hundred-and-twenty-day payment cycles are common and a company can book a record quarter and run out of working capital in the same quarter. The expert tracks contracted, consumed and collected as three separate series and will not sign a compensation plan that pays fully on the first.

The middle stage — between roughly ₹40 crore and ₹200 crore of revenue — is where most of the damage in this discipline is done, because it is the stage at which a company has enough money to hire a sales organisation and not yet enough data to know what to ask it to do. This is where the Sales Learning Curve argument bites hardest: Leslie and Holloway's central prescription was to hire sales capacity slowly until the yield per seller demonstrably exceeds the fully loaded cost per seller, and then to hire aggressively, because hiring ahead of the curve consumes cash at exactly the moment when learning, not capacity, is the constraint. Laghima hired four sellers in one year on a plan that assumed the learning was already complete. It was not.

At large scale the motion becomes an operations problem rather than a selling problem. A mature company runs several motions concurrently, segmented by account size and by product line, with explicit rules governing movement between them, and the hardest question shifts from "should we have sellers" to "which of our seven overlapping teams owns this account, and what happens to the compensation when two of them touch the same deal." That is a governance question, and it is the reason large sales organisations have deal desks, territory carve rules and a compensation committee.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Laghima Robotics: a good motion mis-measured

Laghima's eighteen months produced ₹18.3 crore of bookings at a cost of ₹14.9 crore, which reads as a disaster. Decomposed, it reads differently. Eighteen deals closed at an average of ₹1.02 crore. Gross profit per deal, counting one-time hardware margin at 27% and recurring software margin at 84%, was approximately ₹45 lakh in year one and ₹18.5 lakh a year thereafter. Cost of sale per closed deal was ₹31 lakh including allocated marketing. On a first-year basis the motion paid back; on a recurring-only basis it takes twenty months, which is at the outer edge of what a board with a three-year horizon will tolerate but is not a failure. Two deals discounted to 35% were genuinely value-destroying and should never have been approved. The real finding is that the motion was roughly as productive as an honest model would have predicted and was being managed as though it were failing, which was generating precisely the behaviours — deep discounting, forecast sandbagging, attrition among the two people who actually knew how to sell robots — that would make it fail in year three.

8.2 Lipika Intelligence: the right motion, the wrong instrument

Lipika's problem was never that it had sellers. Regulated lenders will not onboard a document-processing vendor without a human counterparty who can sit through a third-party risk assessment; the political and actuarial rationales for a seller are intact. Lipika's problem was that it had attached a seat-era compensation instrument to a consumption-era product, and the instrument was optimising for the wrong quantity. Eleven accounts, ₹4.2 crore contracted, ₹1.85 crore consumed, ₹37.8 lakh of commission paid.

The remedy Sundaram eventually proposed was not to cut commission but to re-base it: 55% of quota credit on contracted value at signature, 45% on consumption measured at month nine, with the second tranche paid when measured rather than accrued. The immediate effect was that sellers stopped competing to sign the largest possible commitment and started competing to sign commitments the customer would actually consume, which meant the discovery conversation changed from "what is your annual document volume" to "which three document types will you actually route through this in the first quarter, and who owns that migration." The number of accounts fell. Realised revenue per account rose 34% over the following two quarters, and the renewal conversation at Lopamudra Finserv, which had been heading toward a downward renegotiation, converted instead into a smaller committed minimum with an uncapped overage rate — less contracted value on paper, more collected cash.

8.3 Latika Retail Cloud: the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Latika Retail Cloud, a Gurugram company selling store-operations software to retail chains, reached ₹61 crore of ARR almost entirely through self-serve and inside sales, at an average contract value of ₹3.4 lakh. In January 2024 its board, persuaded by a benchmark deck showing that comparable companies at that revenue derived a third of ARR from enterprise accounts, approved an enterprise build-out. Latika hired a VP of Sales from a company that sold ₹4-crore deals, and eight account executives in a single quarter.

Eighteen months later the enterprise motion had consumed ₹14.2 crore and closed nine deals totalling ₹6.1 crore of contract value, of which four, worth ₹2.9 crore, churned at first renewal. Three things had gone wrong and they compounded. First, there was no enterprise ideal customer profile; "enterprise" had been defined as "large retailer," which in India spans organisations with wholly different buying behaviour. Second, the product lacked the institutional apparatus — single sign-on, provisioning, an audit log, a data-residency story adequate to the obligations large buyers were beginning to impose after the Digital Personal Data Protection Act — so every deal either died at security review or survived only because an account executive promised a roadmap. Third, honouring those promises consumed 41% of two quarters of engineering capacity for nine accounts, during which net new self-serve ARR fell from ₹1.9 crore a quarter to ₹1.1 crore. The true cost was therefore not ₹14.2 crore but closer to ₹20 crore once forgone self-serve growth is counted, and that second component never appeared in any review.

The recovery is more instructive than the failure. Latika did not abandon the enterprise ambition; it re-scoped it. It cut to two account executives. It redefined its target band as ₹18–40 lakh rather than ₹1 crore-plus, which Figure 2's arithmetic supports as an inside-sales band and not a field band, and it moved both remaining sellers to an inside model with travel only for late-stage meetings. It built a trigger-based sales-assisted layer on top of self-serve, so that accounts crossing a usage threshold were contacted by a human rather than pursued cold. And critically, it took the institutional apparatus the enterprise motion had demanded — single sign-on, audit logging, role-based access — and shipped it as a paid compliance tier available to the entire base rather than as bespoke work for nine accounts. Roughly 7% of the self-serve base attached that tier, which converted a cost centre into a product line. Fourteen months later Latika had ₹19 crore of ARR in the ₹18–40 lakh band with a CAC payback of sixteen months.

The lesson Latika's CEO drew, and repeated in every subsequent board meeting, was that the original error was not hiring sellers. It was importing a definition of "enterprise" from a benchmark rather than deriving it from the arithmetic of its own cost of sale.
