The pattern across these six is that every one of them is detectable within a single quarter and typically discovered after four. The reason is structural rather than negligent: each failure mode is visible only in a number that crosses an organisational boundary. Mean-versus-median attainment sits between sales operations and finance. Consumption-versus-commitment sits between sales and revenue accounting. Roadmap capture sits between product and sales. Nobody's dashboard spans the seam, so nobody sees the number, so the failure is discovered when its consequence — a missed quarter, a churned cohort, a stalled product — becomes large enough to be visible on one side alone.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does product-led growth make sales-led growth obsolete, or does it feed it? The strong obsolescence position, held by a minority of serious practitioners, is that every function a seller performs is being decomposed: product analytics tell the buyer what a discovery call used to, self-service trials do what a proof of concept used to, public trust centres and machine-readable security documentation do what a security questionnaire used to, and standardised terms do what a redline negotiation used to. On this view, the residual seller is a signature-collector whose numbers will fall by an order of magnitude over a decade, and the buyer-preference survey data pointing to substantial rep-free purchase preference is early evidence. The opposing position holds that this confuses the information problem, which technology is genuinely solving, with the accountability problem, which it is not: a person who signs a ₹4-crore multi-year commitment wants a counterparty who can be summoned when it goes wrong, and no trust centre provides that. For the obsolescence position to be wrong, we would need to see enterprise deal sizes continue rising while seller headcount per crore of revenue stays flat; for it to be right, we would need to see the rep-free preference show up in completed large purchases rather than in stated preference, which so far it has not.

Should the first enterprise seller be a hire or a founder? The hiring position argues that founders systematically mis-learn from their own selling, because they can close deals no employee can replicate — a founder's roadmap promise is credible in a way a seller's is not — and therefore founder-led selling produces a playbook that does not transfer. The founder position argues that the first fifteen cycles are research and cannot be delegated, because the person doing them must have the authority to change the product in response to what they learn, which an account executive does not. Both positions rest on real evidence and the disagreement is probably resolvable only by specifying the product: where the product is nearly complete and the learning is about the buying process, hire; where the learning is still about what the product should be, do not.

Is a wide spread in quota attainment a coaching problem or a selection problem? The coaching camp points to the process school's evidence that documented stage models with exit criteria raise win rates across the whole distribution, and argues that persistent dispersion indicates a management failure to enforce process. The selection camp points to the insight school's finding that performance profiles differ in kind, not degree, and argues that dispersion is evidence the hiring bar is being applied inconsistently — that you cannot coach a relationship-builder into a challenger. The practical stakes are high: one view says invest in enablement, the other says invest in recruiting and manage out faster. What would settle it is longitudinal data on whether individual sellers' attainment percentile is stable across companies, and that data is closely held where it exists at all.

Should product management ever be compensated on bookings? The case for is that the seam in Figure 3 exists because nobody's incentive spans it, and that a product leader with skin in the revenue number will prioritise the enterprise apparatus that unblocks deals rather than treating it as tax. The case against is that it converts the one function whose job is to represent the absent customer — the four thousand self-serve accounts at Latika, who have no seller advocating for them — into another advocate for the loudest present customer. The strongest version of the against case is Latika's own: the forgone self-serve growth was larger than the enterprise spend and had no defender in any room.

Is discounting a pricing failure or a legitimate instrument? One camp treats every discount as evidence that the list price was wrong or the value was not established, and points out that discounts anchor the customer's expectation permanently. The other treats discounting as the only practical mechanism of price discrimination available to a company that cannot publish different prices to different buyers, and notes that the alternative — a rigid list price — simply cedes price-sensitive segments to competitors. Table 2 does not settle this argument but it constrains it: the case for discretionary discounting is far stronger in a high-gross-margin software business than in a bill-of-materials business, and companies that hold the same position across both are not reasoning, they are inheriting a policy.

In AI-native products, should the contract be a commitment or a consumption rate? The commitment camp argues that without a floor, revenue is unforecastable, sales cannot be compensated, and the company cannot plan capacity for its own inference costs. The consumption camp argues that a commitment the customer does not consume is a liability disguised as an asset: it poisons the renewal, it misdirects the sales conversation toward volume projections nobody can make honestly, and it hides the fact that the product has not yet been adopted. Lipika's experience supports the consumption camp; a company with heavy fixed inference-capacity commitments of its own would reasonably reach the opposite conclusion. The disagreement is genuine and currently unresolved, and anyone who tells a product manager there is a settled answer in 2026 is selling something.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can name the stages, recite the qualification frameworks, and compute sales velocity. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They ask about distributions rather than averages, reflexively and in every context — attainment, deal size, supplier GMV, consumption ratio — because they have been burned by a mean at least once and they know that almost every quantity in this discipline is skewed. They treat the composition of the buying committee as a product specification rather than as sales trivia, and they will spend engineering effort to remove an approver in preference to spending sales effort to charm one. They separate contracted, consumed and collected as a matter of habit, and they are physically uncomfortable in a meeting where only the first is on the slide. And they can say, for any given deal, which of the five rationales in section 2 explains why a human being is involved — and they notice when it changes, because a deal that started as an informational sale and has become an actuarial one needs a different closing strategy, different artefacts and, frequently, a different person in the room.

There is a fifth marker, harder to describe. Experts in this discipline are unusually willing to conclude that the motion should be smaller. The gravitational pull of a sales organisation is always toward more headcount, because more headcount is the only lever a sales leader unambiguously controls, and because the arithmetic that would justify restraint lives in finance. The practitioner who can hold the Figure 2 thresholds in mind and say, in a board meeting, that the correct number of field sellers for a ₹30 lakh average contract is zero, is doing something that the structure of the organisation actively discourages.

12. What they decided

Mahajan went to Laghima's board on 4 September 2025 with a rebuilt model rather than a recommendation, which is itself instructive. He presented Table 1 in both columns and argued that the company had not run a failed experiment but an unmeasured one, and that the first decision was to re-base the plan honestly before deciding anything about headcount. He proposed holding the team at six sellers for two more quarters — neither doubling nor cutting — while spending ₹2.4 crore of engineering capacity on three specific items chosen because each removed an approval gate rather than because a customer asked: software-configurable exclusion zones to retire the insurer's surveyor, a hardened network appliance with a published security posture to retire the group CISO's bespoke review, and a robots-as-a-service commercial structure to collapse the capex and opex approval paths into one. He also withdrew discount authority above 15% from the VP of Sales and expressed the remaining authority in gross-profit rupees. His argument to the board was that at eleven gates the company's win rate was arithmetically capped regardless of who it hired, and that the cheapest available unit of win rate was engineering, not headcount. The board approved it, with a condition Mahajan had not asked for: a quarterly review of the promise ledger, presented jointly by him and the VP of Sales.

Sundaram's decision at Lipika was narrower and harder, because it required taking money away from people who had earned it under the rules as written. She re-based the compensation plan to 55% contracted and 45% consumed-at-month-nine, grandfathered the existing cohort rather than clawing back, and accepted a quarter of depressed bookings as the price. She also made a product decision that Kulkarni opposed: Lipika began publishing consumption dashboards to customers, including a projection of whether they were on track to use their committed minimum. Kulkarni's objection was that this handed the customer the argument for a smaller renewal. Sundaram's position was that the customer would discover the shortfall at renewal in any case, and that discovering it in month four with a Lipika engineer available to fix the migration bottleneck was a fundamentally different conversation from discovering it in month eleven with a true-up invoice attached. Neither of them believed they had persuaded the other.

Questions for discussion

  1. Mahajan chose to spend ₹2.4 crore of engineering capacity on removing approval gates rather than on features customers had requested. Under what conditions is that the wrong trade — and how would a product leader know, in advance, that they had crossed into building for procurement rather than for users?
  2. Laghima's board was shown a capacity plan built on mean attainment and approved it. Lipika's board approved a commission plan built for a seat-based product. In both cases the error was in an instrument rather than in a decision. Who in a company is accountable for the correctness of instruments, and what would it take for that accountability to be real?
  3. Latika recovered by redefining "enterprise" from ₹1 crore-plus to ₹18–40 lakh. That redefinition was arithmetically correct and strategically humbling. If you were the CEO presenting it, what evidence would you need to distinguish a disciplined retreat from an abandoned ambition — and would that distinction survive contact with an investor who had funded the original plan?

13. Going deeper

What a GTM strategy is
The frame within which sales-led growth is one option among several; without it, the motion decision gets made by whoever hires first. It unlocks the ability to state a segment, a motion and a price as one coherent choice rather than three independent ones.
Product-led sales (PQA / PQL)
The mechanism that connects self-serve usage signals to a human seller, and the direct answer to Latika's recovery problem. It unlocks a sales-assisted layer that costs a fraction of a field motion and can be triggered by behaviour rather than by cold targeting.
Choosing the GTM motion
The decision procedure behind Figure 2's thresholds, applied per segment rather than per company. It unlocks the discipline of running two or three motions concurrently with explicit rules for moving accounts between them.
Working with sales
The operational practice at Figure 3's seams — the promise ledger, the deal desk, the roadmap-capture ratio. It unlocks the ability to be useful in a deal without becoming an unpaid account executive.
Your first 100 users
The stage before a motion exists, where founder-led selling is research rather than revenue. It unlocks the written qualification criteria without which any first sales hire is being asked to do archaeology.
Channels: paid, owned, earned
Where the pipeline that a sales-led motion consumes actually comes from, and why a field team without a channel strategy becomes an expensive outbound team. It unlocks the cost-per-qualified-opportunity number that sits underneath every cost-of-sale calculation in this page.
Inbound vs outbound
The distinction that determines whether cycle time is set by the buyer's trigger or by the seller's persistence, and therefore whether the Table 1 ramp assumptions hold. It unlocks realistic ramp modelling for a new territory.
Product-led growth
The motion this one is defined against, and the source of the strongest argument that sales-led growth is a transitional artefact. It unlocks the ability to steelman the obsolescence position in section 10 rather than dismissing it.
Launch planning and launch mistakes
Where the enterprise apparatus — security posture, references, redline bank — either exists at launch or is discovered missing at the first security review. It unlocks a launch checklist that includes the things procurement will ask for, not only the things users will.
Crossing the chasm
Geoffrey Moore's account of why the buyers who will take a risk on you are structurally different from the buyers who will not, which is the deepest available explanation for why Latika's enterprise deals died at security review. It unlocks the segment-first discipline that Latika's recovery amounted to rediscovering.
